    Managing Containers

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do I view all containers on my system, including those that have stopped?
    • How do I run a container in the background and still access its output?
    • How can I execute commands or open a shell inside a running container?
    • How do I share files between my host machine and a container?
    • How do I remove containers and images when they are no longer needed?

    Objectives

    • Use podman commands for listing, starting, stopping, and removing containers and images.
    • Explain the difference between podman run and podman container start.
    • Interpret container exit codes and explain what they indicate.
    • Run a long-lived service container in detached mode with a published port.
    • Use podman exec to run commands and open an interactive shell inside a running container.
    • Mount a host directory into a container using the -v option to share files.
    • Determine the correct order of operations for removing containers and their associated images.

    Inspecting Images and Containers

    Now that we’ve downloaded and run our first container, we can inspect the images and containers stored on our system.

    To see the images currently available, run:

    BASH 

    podman image list

    OUTPUT 

    REPOSITORY            TAG         IMAGE ID      CREATED      SIZE
quay.io/podman/hello  latest      83fc7ce1224f  2 years ago  580 kB

    This shows the hello image that Podman downloaded when we ran the container. Notice the CREATED column. This refers to when the image was created and published by its developer, and not when it was downloaded onto your computer.

    If we now list our running containers:

    BASH 

    podman container list

    OUTPUT 

    CONTAINER ID  IMAGE       COMMAND     CREATED     STATUS      PORTS       NAMES

    It may seem odd that the output is empty. Although we just ran a container, this command only displays currently running containers. Our hello container simply started, printed its message, and then exited immediately. This highlights an important characteristic of containers: they do not need to be long-running services. Many containers are designed as one-shot programs that perform a task and then terminate.

    To view all containers, including those that have already stopped, use the --all option:

    BASH 

    podman container list --all

    Or equivalently:

    BASH 

    podman container list -a

    OUTPUT 

    CONTAINER ID  IMAGE                        COMMAND               CREATED        STATUS                    PORTS       NAMES
2a2af201f219  quay.io/podman/hello:latest  /usr/local/bin/po...  4 minutes ago  Exited (0) 4 minutes ago              confident_solomon

    This time you’ll see the container that was created a few moments ago. Notice that its status is shown as Exited (0). The value in parentheses is the container’s exit code:

    • An exit code of 0 indicates that the container completed successfully..
    • An exit code of 1 or otherwise would indicate the container exited prematurely due to an error.

    The name confident_solomon name is randomly assigned as a human-readable identifier for the container.

    Naming Containers

    Another useful column is NAMES. By default, Podman assigns each new container a randomly generated name consisting of two words. This gives us a convenient way to refer to the container later, but remembering randomly assigned names can quickly become inconvenient.

    A more predictable approach is to assign your own name when creating the container by using the --name option:

    BASH 

    podman run --name hello_world quay.io/podman/hello

    This time you’ll notice that Podman does not download the image again, because it is already stored locally. You can confirm this by running:

    BASH 

    podman image list

    There is still only a single hello image. However, if you list all containers again:

    BASH 

    podman container list -a

    OUTPUT 

    CONTAINER ID  IMAGE                        COMMAND               CREATED        STATUS                    PORTS       NAMES
2a2af201f219  quay.io/podman/hello:latest  /usr/local/bin/po...  6 minutes ago  Exited (0) 6 minutes ago              confident_solomon
15731f65ecfe  quay.io/podman/hello:latest  /usr/local/bin/po...  7 seconds ago  Exited (0) 7 seconds ago              hello_world

    You’ll now see two containers. Although both were created from the same image, each execution of podman run creates a new container. The second container uses the name we explicitly assigned, i.e. hello_world.

    Restarting an Existing Container

    Rather than creating a new container every time, we can start an existing one again using podman container start:

    BASH 

    podman container start hello_world

    OUTPUT 

    hello_world

    The container does run, but only the container name appears on the terminal. This is because podman container start starts the container without attaching its standard input and output to the current terminal.

    When we originally used podman run, the terminal was attached automatically, allowing us to see the program’s output. To achieve the same behaviour when restarting an existing container, add the --attach option:

    BASH 

    podman container start --attach hello_world

    This reruns the existing container and displays its output in the terminal.

    Using podman run again would create another new container, whereas podman container start allows us to rerun one that already exists.

    Command Shortcuts

    Typing podman container before every command quickly becomes repetitive, so Podman provides convenient shortcuts for many common operations.

    For example, instead of:

    BASH 

    podman container start --attach hello_world

    you can simply write:

    BASH 

    podman start --attach hello_world

    Likewise, to stop a long-running container (which we’ll encounter later), you can use:

    BASH 

    podman stop <container-name>

    instead of:

    BASH 

    podman container stop <container-name>

    Similar shortcuts are available for several other frequently used Podman commands.

    Removing Containers and Images

    As we continue working with containers, we’ll gradually accumulate images and containers on our system. Some of these may no longer be useful, so it’s important to know how to remove them and reclaim disk space.

    Let’s start by looking at the images we currently have:

    BASH 

    podman image list

    Suppose we decide to remove the hello image. We can do that using the image rm command, where rm is short for remove:

    BASH 

    podman image rm quay.io/podman/hello

    However, this doesn’t succeed. Podman reports an error because the image is still being used by one or more containers. Before an image can be deleted, every container based on that image must first be removed.

    To see the containers currently on our system, including those that have already stopped, run:

    BASH 

    podman container list -a

    Our first container was given a randomly generated name by Podman. Remove it using the name shown on your own system. For example:

    BASH 

    podman container rm confident_solomon

    Your container will almost certainly have a different name. If the command succeeds, Podman prints the container’s unique identifier, confirming that it has been removed.

    We can then remove the second container, which we explicitly named hello_world:

    BASH 

    podman container rm hello_world

    Verify that both containers have been removed:

    BASH 

    podman container list -a

    With no remaining containers using the image, we can now remove the image itself:

    BASH 

    podman image rm quay.io/podman/hello

    Podman confirms that the image has been deleted. We can verify this by listing the remaining images:

    BASH 

    podman image list

    At this point we’ve removed all of the containers and images created during the earlier exercises.

    Running a Web Server Container

    So far we’ve only run a simple “Hello World” container. Let’s now run something a little more useful by starting a web server inside a container.

    Type in the following command, but do not yet press Enter:

    BASH 

    podman run --name webserver -p 8080:80/tcp docker.io/library/httpd

    Several things are happening here:

    • --name webserver gives the container a meaningful name, which we’ve seen before.
    • docker.io/library/httpd specifies the image to download and run. In this case the image comes from the Docker Hub (docker.io) registry, demonstrating that Podman can use Docker images directly.
    • The image contains an Apache HTTP Server, httpd.
    • The -p option publishes a network port, allowing software running inside the container to be accessed from the host machine.

    The port mapping is written as host-port:container-port/protocol. In this example:

    • The web server listens on port 80 inside the container
    • That port is mapped to port 8080 on the host
    • The connection uses the TCP protocol

    Web servers typically listen on port 80, but using port 8080 on the host avoids conflicts with any web server already running on your machine and avoids the elevated privileges often required for low-numbered ports.

    Now press Enter to download and start the container.

    Unlike our hello example, this container continues running. The terminal remains attached to the container, displaying the Apache log output as requests are received.

    Accessing the Web Server

    Once the container is running, open a web browser and visit http://localhost:8080

    You should see a page displaying the message It works!.

    If you watch the terminal running the container, you’ll also see Apache log the request. This is exactly what we’d expect from a normal web server.

    You can also retrieve the page directly from another terminal. Start another terminal, but be careful not to resize the terminal with the running webserver within it, since this may send SIGWINCH (signal of window change) to that terminal, and cause the container to exit.

    On macOS, Windows, or Linux with curl installed, run:

    BASH 

    curl http://localhost:8080

    The HTML source of the page is displayed in the terminal:

    OUTPUT 

    <!DOCTYPE HTML PUBLIC "-//W3C//DTD HTML 4.01//EN" "http://www.w3.org/TR/html4/strict.dtd">
<html>
<head>
<title>It works! Apache httpd</title>
</head>
<body>
<p>It works!</p>
</body>
</html>

    If curl is not available, Linux users can use wget instead:

    BASH 

    wget -nv -O - http://localhost:8080

    The additional options tell wget to:

    • Suppress most status output (-nv)
    • Write the downloaded page to standard output instead of a file (-O -)

    The result is essentially the same HTML page, together with a brief status message.

    Running Containers in the Background

    Having the web server occupy an entire terminal isn’t always convenient. Fortunately, containers can also run in detached mode, allowing them to continue running in the background.

    First, stop the existing container from another terminal:

    BASH 

    podman stop webserver

    This uses the shortcut form of podman container stop. The terminal running the web server should display log messages indicating that Apache is shutting down, after which the container exits.

    We can then remove the stopped container:

    BASH 

    podman rm webserver

    Now from within the original terminal that we used to start the container, rerun the web server in detached mode:

    BASH 

    podman run --name webserver -dt -p 8080:80/tcp docker.io/library/httpd

    The additional -dt options change how the container runs:

    • -d starts the container in the background, in a detached state
    • -t allocates a pseudo-terminal so that the container’s output is retained internally for logging purposes

    This time the command immediately returns to the shell while the web server continues running in the background, leaving the terminal free for other work.

    Viewing Container Logs

    When a container is running in detached mode, it no longer writes its output directly to the terminal. While this keeps the terminal free for other work, it also means we can no longer see what the application inside the container is doing.

    Fortunately, Podman stores the container’s output and allows us to view it at any time using the logs command:

    BASH 

    podman logs webserver

    This displays the web server’s log output, allowing us to inspect recent activity without needing to restart or reattach to the container.

    Running Commands Inside a Running Container

    Viewing logs is useful, but sometimes we need much greater access to a running container. For example, we may want to inspect its filesystem, check configuration files, or run diagnostic commands.

    Podman provides the exec command, which executes a command inside an already running container.

    For example, to list the contents of the root directory of the container, run:

    BASH 

    podman exec -ti webserver /bin/ls /

    OUTPUT 

    bin   dev  home  media	opt   root  sbin  sys  usr
boot  etc  lib	 mnt	proc  run   srv   tmp  var

    Here:

    • exec executes a command inside the container
    • -t allocates a terminal
    • -i keeps standard input open, allowing interactive commands

    We can also see the container’s current working directory:

    BASH 

    podman exec -ti webserver /bin/pwd

    OUTPUT 

    /usr/local/apache2

    This shows that commands execute from the Apache web server’s working directory.

    Opening an Interactive Shell

    Running individual commands with podman exec is useful, but repeatedly typing long commands soon becomes tedious.

    Instead, we can start an interactive shell inside the container:

    BASH 

    podman exec -ti webserver /bin/bash

    OUTPUT 

    root@e7af92db948c:/usr/local/apache2#

    This gives us a shell prompt inside the running container, allowing us to explore it much as we would a remote machine accessed via SSH.

    Notice that we are logged in as the root user within the container, so we have full administrative privileges over the container’s filesystem.

    For example, we can locate the web page that Apache is serving:

    BASH 

    ls

    OUTPUT 

    bin  build  cgi-bin  conf  error  htdocs  icons  include  logs	modules

    BASH 

    cd htdocs

    We can also look at the HTML document that was served to us earlier:

    BASH 

    cat index.html

    OUTPUT 

    <!DOCTYPE HTML PUBLIC "-//W3C//DTD HTML 4.01//EN" "http://www.w3.org/TR/html4/strict.dtd">
<html>
<head>
<title>It works! Apache httpd</title>
</head>
<body>
<p>It works!</p>
</body>
</html>

    When you’ve finished exploring, exit the shell as normal:

    BASH 

    exit

    You’ll be returned to your host machine’s command prompt.

    Stopping and Removing the Container

    Because the web server is running in detached mode, we can stop it from the same terminal:

    BASH 

    podman stop webserver

    Once it has stopped, remove it as before:

    BASH 

    podman container rm webserver

    You can verify that it has been removed by listing all containers:

    BASH 

    podman container list -a

    The webserver container should no longer appear in the list.

    Sharing Files Between the Host and a Container

    So far we’ve treated containers as self-contained environments. However, real-world applications almost always need to exchange data with their host system.

    For example, suppose we’re running a scientific analysis inside a container because it provides the correct software environment. We’ll need a way to provide the analysis with input data and retrieve the results afterwards.

    Fortunately, Podman makes this straightforward.

    Just as we previously mapped a host network port to a container port, we can also mount a directory from the host machine inside the container. This allows the host and container to access the same files.

    Let’s demonstrate this by serving our own web page from the host machine using the Apache web server container.

    Create a Web Content Directory on the Host

    First, create a directory to hold our web pages:

    BASH 

    mkdir webdocs

    Next, create a simple HTML page inside that directory using your preferred text editor.

    For example, using Nano:

    BASH 

    nano webdocs/index.html

    Add a very simple page:

    HTML 

    <html><body>Hello there!</body></html>

    Feel free to replace the text with your own message.

    If you’re using Nano, press Ctrl+O to save the file and Ctrl+X to exit. On Windows, you can use Notepad or any other text editor to create the same file.

    Mounting a Host Directory

    We can now start a new web server container, this time giving it access to the webdocs directory we created on our host machine.

    The command differs slightly depending on your operating system, because we’ll use an environment variable to refer to our current working directory. Windows and Linux/macOS use different syntax for environment variables.

    If you’re using Windows with the Command Prompt, use:

    BASH 

    podman run --name webserver -v %CD%/webdocs:/usr/local/apache2/htdocs -dt -p 8080:80/tcp docker.io/library/httpd

    If you’re using Linux, MacOS, or Windows with Git Bash, use:

    BASH 

    podman run --name webserver -v $PWD/webdocs:/usr/local/apache2/htdocs -dt -p 8080:80/tcp docker.io/library/httpd

    Don’t press Enter immediately, let’s first examine the new part of the command.

    The command is almost identical to the one we used previously, except for the addition of the -v option. This option creates a volume mount, allowing a directory on the host machine to be accessed from within the container.

    The general form is: -v <host-directory>:<container-directory>

    The first path specifies the directory on the host, while the second specifies where that directory will appear inside the container.

    For the host directory, we need to provide its full path. Rather than typing this manually, we use an environment variable representing the current directory:

    • $PWD on Linux, MacOS, and Git Bash
    • %CD% on Windows Command Prompt

    Appending /webdocs gives the full path to the directory we created earlier.

    The second path /usr/local/apache2/htdocs is where the Apache web server stores the web pages it serves. By mounting our webdocs directory here, the container sees our local files instead of its own default web pages.

    In effect, whenever Apache reads files from its htdocs directory, it is actually reading the contents of the webdocs directory on the host machine.

    Now press Enter to start the container.

    As before, Podman immediately returns the container’s unique identifier, indicating that the container has started successfully in detached mode.

    Verifying the Mounted Files

    To confirm that the container is serving our own web page, visit http://localhost:8080 in a web browser.

    Alternatively, you can retrieve the page from the command line using curl:

    BASH 

    curl http://localhost:8080

    This time, instead of the default Apache “It works!” page, you should see the HTML that you created in webdocs/index.html.

    This demonstrates one of the most useful features of containers: applications running inside a container can work directly with files on the host machine, making it easy to edit data locally while software inside the container uses it immediately.

    Key Points
    • podman container list -a shows all containers including stopped ones whilst podman container list shows only running containers.
    • An exit code of 0 means a container completed successfully, whereas a non-zero exit code indicates an error.
    • podman run always creates a new container, and podman container start restarts an existing stopped container.
    • The -p host-port:container-port/protocol option maps a port inside a container to a port on the host, enabling access to services running in the container.
    • The -d flag runs a container in detached (background) mode.
    • podman logs <name> retrieves the log output from a running (background) container.
    • podman exec -ti <container> /bin/bash opens an interactive shell inside a running container.
    • The -v <host-dir>:<container-dir> option mounts a host directory into the container, allowing both to access the same files.
    • All containers based on an image must be removed before that image can be deleted.
